title: Annotatio I §.IV cont: Picherellus — Tertullian’s quasi vere; Origen, Augustine, Cyril on figurative eating
pass_a_gloss: I judge it worth the work to recite this man’s words, both because the man’s Opuscula are in very few hands, and because the Author deserves so much the greater faith the more the Pontificians commonly press the propriety of Christ’s words more closely: When Christ said in John 6, says Picherellus, Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man &c., Tertullian (On the Resurrection of the Flesh, marg. no. 28) understands that He said His flesh was to be eaten not truly (i.e. improperly) — they judged His speech hard and intolerable, as if He had truly determined His flesh to be eaten by them. These words as if truly make Tertullian to have understood not truly. To whom Origen on Leviticus ch. 7 agrees (cited de consecr. dist. 2 can. de hac): Of this host which is wonderfully made in Christ’s commemoration it is lawful to eat; but of that which Christ offered on the altar of the cross it is not lawful to eat according to itself. And to that mode, because by this saying Christ seems to command a crime or outrage, Augustine says the locution is figurative (On Christian Doctrine bk. 3 ch. 16; On Faith against the Manichees ch. 37–38); and Cyril also acknowledges it figurative in book 7 on Leviticus.
pass_b_english: Picherellus is worth quoting: few own his Opuscula, and a Pontifician witness carries extra weight when his own side presses Christ’s words as proper.

On John 6’s Unless you eat the flesh… he reads Tertullian as taking the eating not truly — i.e. improperly — because the hearers treated the sermon as hard as if He had truly set His flesh to be eaten (quasi vere → non vere).
Origen, Augustine, and Cyril likewise mark figurative speech for that hard saying.
source_text: Hujus Verba recitare operae pretium duco, tùm quòd Opuscula viri in paucorum admodum manibus versantur, tùm quòd tantò majorem fidem meretur Autor, quantò Pontificii communiter proprietatem verborum Christi pressius urgere consuevere: Cum diceret Christus Joh. 6., inquit Picherellus, nisi carnem filii hominis manducaveritis &c. intelligit Tertullianus lib. de resurrect. carnis, num. marg. 28. non verè (i. e. improprie) dixisse edendam carnem suam, durum inquit & intolerabilem existimaverunt sermonem ejus, quasi verè carnem suam illis edendam determinasset. Voces hae quasi verè, faciunt ut Tertullianus intellexerit non verè. Cui adstipulatur Origenes in Lev. cap. 7timum, qui citatur de consecr. dist. 2 can. de hac. De hac hostia, quae in Christi commemorationem mirabiliter fit, edere licet: de illa verò, quam Christus in ara crucis obtulit, secundum se edere non licet. Ad eumque modum, quia videtur hoc dicto Christus facinus vel flagitium jubere, Augustinus ait figuratam esse locutionem, de doctr. Christ. lib. 3. cap. 16. & de fide contra Manich. cap. 37. 38. & figuratam etiam agnoscit Cyrillus in libro 7timo ad Leviticum.
